Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 54: Measuring Performance
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. Measure a named boundary before comparing numbers
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A benchmark number has little meaning until we know what happened inside its boundary. A request's latency might include waiting in a queue, parsing, computation, and delivery, while a kernel benchmark may time only one prepared loop. Throughput counts completed useful work over an elapsed interval. CPU time counts processor execution under the operating system's accounting rules. These are not interchangeable units of success. This chapter uses both actual timing mechanics and explicitly supplied observations. When we calculate a model result, we will label it as such rather than pretending that deterministic output is a measurement of this machine.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.004: 54.1 Latency

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Concurrent request durations are not the elapsed interval
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Our supplied observations describe three requests that all begin at zero and complete at ten milliseconds. Adding their durations produces thirty milliseconds of request time, but the observed wall interval is only ten. Dividing three by that actual interval gives three hundred completions per second. The incorrect serial assumption gives one hundred. The program prints both calculations and labels the sum-based one wrong. These are arithmetic over a stated fixture, not timings collected by the program. This distinction matters whenever requests overlap: throughput needs a completion count and an elapsed observation window, not the sum of individual response durations.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.006: 54.2 Throughput

------------------------------------------------------------

3. One average can hide very different users’ waits
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This supplied sample has nine quick requests and one slow request. The total is one hundred milliseconds across ten observations, giving a mean of ten. After sorting, the lower central observation is one, and both middle observations are one, so the median is one. Under the nearest-rank percentile rule, the ninety-fifth percentile selects rank ten and is ninety-one. The output makes the long tail visible, but ten samples do not establish a reliable population tail estimate. A percentile needs a stated definition, sample count, and representative workload. Sorting a local vector is acceptable here because the fixture's original order is not needed later.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

4. CPU seconds can exceed elapsed seconds
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A four-thread computation can use roughly four CPU seconds during one second of elapsed time if all four run continuously on separate cores. That is not a broken clock; CPU time adds execution charged across threads. Conversely, a job can take two wall seconds while using only six-tenths of a CPU second because it waits for I/O or scheduling. The difference suggests where to investigate, but does not identify one cause by itself. Helper processes and kernel accounting boundaries can also matter. Record whether your number covers one thread, one process, or the complete multi-process job.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
Dividing by 15 without converting milliseconds to seconds gives a value per millisecond, not per second.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Report 3/15 as requests per second. The denominator is milliseconds, so the units are wrong by a factor of 1000.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Convert the interval to seconds and state the percentile convention. Preserve raw measurements for later checks.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
The mean describes total time divided by count; the selected percentile describes an order statistic. Sorting a copy preserves the caller’s sample order. Three observations make a very weak basis for real tail-latency inference: the example teaches the calculation, not statistical confidence. Throughput here uses a serial interval; concurrent request durations cannot simply be added to infer wall time.

A plausible alternative: A checksum or observable result keeps benchmark work relevant, but timing still needs warmup, repetitions, and controlled comparisons.

8. Chapter 54 — Measuring Performance
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Performance engineering begins by defining the work and the measurement boundary. A number is meaningful only when it identifies what completed, under which conditions, and how the observation was made. Correctness checks belong in the experiment: a program that skips work can appear extraordinarily fast. This chapter distinguishes measured observations , analytical models , and illustrative assumptions . The companion benchmark reports local timings when run, but the book does not convert one container run into a universal hardware claim. Reproduce measurements on the machine and workload that matter. [ R30 , R42 ]

10. Latency
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Latency measures elapsed time from a defined start event to a defined completion event. For a request, the boundary might include queueing, parsing, computation, and response delivery. For a kernel, it might include only the computation after inputs are prepared. Report a distribution when requests vary. A mean can hide a long tail, and a percentile requires enough samples and a clearly defined population. Do not compare one system’s median service time with another system’s end-to-end 99th percentile as though they were the same metric.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.004, SP54.005

------------------------------------------------------------

11. Throughput
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Throughput measures completed useful work per unit time. It can be expressed as records, requests, or bytes per second. Define whether failed requests, retries, warmup work, and partial completions count. Throughput and latency interact through queueing. A system can increase completed work by admitting more concurrent requests while making each request wait longer. Evaluate the service objective rather than maximizing a single number without constraints.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

12. CPU time
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
CPU time measures processor execution charged to a process or thread under the operating system’s accounting rules. It excludes many periods spent blocked or not scheduled. A multithreaded process can accumulate more total CPU time than elapsed wall time when several threads execute concurrently. CPU time helps distinguish computation from waiting, but it is not a complete explanation. Kernel activity, helper processes, and accounting boundaries may contribute differently. State whether the measurement covers one thread, the whole process, or a larger job.

DO

13. Wall-clock time
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Wall-clock elapsed time includes waiting, scheduling delays, and other activity between the chosen start and end. For duration measurements, use a monotonic clock such as std::chrono::steady_clock rather than a civil-time clock that can be adjusted. Clock resolution and call overhead matter for very small operations. Batch enough work to make the measured interval meaningful, while ensuring that the batch still represents the workload and does not change cache behavior beyond the intended experiment.

DO

14. Utilization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Utilization describes the fraction of a resource’s capacity in use under a stated definition. CPU utilization, memory bandwidth utilization, and device busy time are different metrics. High CPU utilization does not prove that useful work is progressing efficiently; a spin loop can consume an entire core. Low utilization does not automatically mean spare end-to-end capacity. The bottleneck may be a serialized dependency, a lock, a downstream service, or a limit in another resource. Identify the constrained stage before adding more work.

DO

15. Benchmarking
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A benchmark should state input size and distribution, build configuration, machine context, warmup policy, repetition count, and correctness criteria. Keep setup outside the timed region when the goal excludes setup, and include it when evaluating end-to-end behavior. Preserve observable results so the compiler cannot legally discard the intended work as unused. Inspect generated code when a result seems implausible. Avoid volatile as a blanket benchmarking technique because it can change the workload being measured rather than merely prevent elimination.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.014, SP54.015

16. Measurement error
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Measurements vary because of scheduling, frequency changes, contention, cache state, page faults, thermal behavior, and instrumentation overhead. Repeated samples reveal variation but do not automatically remove bias. Change one factor at a time where practical and alternate comparison order to reduce drift effects. Report uncertainty honestly. A difference smaller than the experiment’s noise is not strong evidence of improvement, and a statistically clear difference may still be too small to matter operationally.

DO

17. A checksum-protected timing boundary
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
This program constructs a bounded runtime-sized vector, times one summation, and verifies the sum against an independent formula. Setup and verification are outside the timed interval. The output timing is an observation on the machine where it is run, not a fixed expected value. Companion listing: ch54/benchmark.cpp For count 1000, there are three complete groups of values 0 through 250 and a remainder of 247 values, 0 through 246. The expected sum is 3 × 31375 + 247 × 246/2 = 124506 . The elapsed nanoseconds vary. A zero or very small reported duration for a tiny input can reflect clock granularity or overhead dominance rather than infinite throughput. The program is a measurement-mechanics example, not a complete microbenchmark framework. Repeat separate runs, record build flags, inspect the loop, and compare like conditions before interpreting a performance difference. Allocation failure is reported by the C++ runtime unless a surrounding application adds a more specific recovery policy.

18. Throughput and latency
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
If a service completes 12,000 requests in 60 seconds, average throughput is 200 requests/s. That fact does not reveal individual latency: one request may complete in 2 ms while another waits 500 ms. Report throughput and latency distributions separately because batching and queueing can improve one while harming the other.

19. CPU time versus wall time
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A task reports 2.0 s wall-clock time but only 0.6 s CPU time. The remaining elapsed time may include waiting for I/O, scheduling delays, or sleeps. Optimizing arithmetic cannot remove time spent blocked on a slow dependency unless the design changes that dependency or overlaps it with other work.

23. A clock read has cost and a limited resolution
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Civil time can be adjusted, so duration measurements should normally use a monotonic clock such as steady_clock. Even that clock has a finite resolution and reading it has overhead. If one operation is extremely short, a measured zero does not imply infinite speed; it may be below the clock's visible scale. Batching operations can enlarge the interval, but also changes cache reuse and amortizes setup. State whether that batch represents the actual requirement. Keep the clock outside the operation only when the boundary excludes its overhead, and compare repeated observations under documented conditions.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.010: 54.4 Wall-clock time

------------------------------------------------------------

24. A benchmark must make the intended work observable
Reason about the implementation

SAY
If a loop computes a result that the program never uses, an optimizing compiler may legally remove it. Timing the empty remainder does not measure the intended calculation. The source benchmark keeps a checksum and compares it with an independent formula after the timed interval. That verifies useful behavior without including verification time in that chosen boundary. Using volatile everywhere is not a general repair because it changes access semantics and may create a different workload. If a result looks implausibly fast, inspect the generated code, build options, input size, and timing boundary before announcing an optimization win.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.018: Worked example — A checksum-protected timing boundary

------------------------------------------------------------

25. High utilization is not proof of useful progress
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A core at one hundred percent can be calculating useful results, spinning on a lock, or repeatedly handling irrelevant events. The utilization number alone cannot distinguish them. Likewise, low CPU use does not mean the service has spare end-to-end capacity: a serialized storage or network dependency may be saturated. Use utilization to guide a hypothesis, then connect it to completions, latency, and queue growth. If adding clients raises CPU use while throughput stays flat and latency rises, more admitted work may simply be increasing contention. The objective is useful completion under constraints, not the highest busy percentage.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.012: 54.5 Utilization

------------------------------------------------------------

26. Control comparisons without hiding variation
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Running version A once on a cool idle machine and B once after background work begins is a weak comparison. Repeat representative runs, record relevant conditions, and alternate ordering when practical to reduce drift. Variation can come from frequency changes, cache state, page faults, scheduling, contention, and instrumentation. Repetition reveals spread but does not automatically remove bias. If an apparent improvement is smaller than the experiment's noise, the evidence is weak. A statistically clear difference can still be operationally unimportant, so report both uncertainty and the size of the effect relevant to users.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

27. Run the complete chapter demonstration
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Three serial requests take 2, 8, and 5 milliseconds. Compute mean latency and throughput over the 15-millisecond interval.

Define the interval. 15 milliseconds, three completed requests. Throughput needs a count and an elapsed-time interval.

Compute the mean. 15 / 3 = 5 milliseconds per request. The mean hides the slow 8-millisecond request.

Convert units. 3 / 0.015 = 200 requests per second. The formula assumes the stated serial interval; concurrent completions require their actual observed interval.

Build the complete demonstration and compare every output character. The separate lab solution includes assertions for its named acceptance checks.

30. Report latency and throughput with units
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Report latency and throughput with units. accumulate sums the three durations with a double initial value. For this serial fixture the total is fifteen milliseconds.

Three serial requests take 2, 8, and 5 milliseconds. Compute mean latency and throughput over the 15-millisecond interval.

Throughput needs a count and an elapsed-time interval. The mean hides the slow 8-millisecond request. The formula assumes the stated serial interval; concurrent completions require their actual observed interval.

accumulate sums the three durations with a double initial value. For this serial fixture the total is fifteen milliseconds.

Divide total duration by three observations to obtain a mean of five milliseconds per request.

Convert milliseconds to seconds before dividing three requests by elapsed time: 3/0.015 = 200 per second. Overlapping request durations cannot be summed to infer real wall-clock throughput.

Duration units and measurement scope are explicit. Summing these durations represents serial elapsed time, not an overlapping concurrent workload.

Dividing by 15 without converting milliseconds to seconds gives a value per millisecond, not per second. In the extended lab: Report 3/15 as requests per second. The denominator is milliseconds, so the units are wrong by a factor of 1000.

42. Keep setup in or out for a stated reason
Recall and transfer

SAY
An optimized index can answer one query quickly after expensive construction. Timing only the query answers one question; timing construction plus the workload answers another. Neither boundary is inherently dishonest if stated clearly, but comparing them as if they were the same is misleading. The chapter's checksum example constructs data before timing because it studies summation mechanics. A file-processing service must also measure reading, allocation, parsing, and final delivery when those are part of the user's wait. Preserve separate measurements if they help diagnose where total time goes, then judge the change against the real objective.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch54.json → SP54.014: 54.6 Benchmarking

------------------------------------------------------------

43. Write the measurement claim so someone can reproduce it
Recall and transfer

SAY
A useful result might say that this build processed this many bounded records, produced this checksum, and completed within a distribution of elapsed times under these conditions. That statement is much stronger than calling an implementation fast. Keep fixture arithmetic, modeled ceilings, and actual clock observations visibly separate. The lecture programs printed fixed statistics because their inputs were supplied; the source timing program prints a duration that varies. In a review, ask whether another person could reproduce the build, input, measurement boundary, and correctness check. If not, improve the experiment before arguing over a small speed difference.

DO
Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
